statement.p: A one-meter long bar is heated unevenly, with temperature in {}^\circC at a distance x meters from one end at time t given by H(x,t) = 140e^{-0.15t}\sin\mathopen{}\left(\pi x\right) 0\le x\le 1. On a sheet of paper, sketch a graph of H against x for t=0 and t=1. Think about why your graphs make sense.

p.em: (Be sure that you can say in words what the practical interpretation (in terms of temperature) of these two partial derivatives is, and why each has the sign that it does.)
(Again, be sure that you understand why it has the sign that it does, and what its interpretation in terms of temperature is.)

static.solution:
t=0 and t=1 into the formula for H gives: H(x,0) = 140e^{0}\sin\mathopen{}\left(\pi x\right), and H(x,1) = 140e^{-0.15}\sin\mathopen{}\left(\pi x\right). The graphs of these are shown below (with H(x,0) in red and H(x,1) in blue).
Note that this makes sense: it says that the bar starts with a varying temperature distribution, and that as time goes on the temperature decays at all points on the bar towards a temperature of zero.
(a) To calculate H_x(x,t), we hold t constant and differentiate with respect to x: H_x(x,t) = \frac{\partial}{\partial x}H(x,t) = \frac{\partial}{\partial x} 140e^{-0.15t}\sin\mathopen{}\left(\pi x\right) = 140e^{-0.15t}\pi \cos\mathopen{}\left(\pi x\right). Thus H_x(0.2,t) = 140\pi e^{-0.15 t}\cos(0.2 \pi) = 140e^{-0.15t}\pi \cos\mathopen{}\left(\pi \cdot 0.2\right)\quad {}^\circ\hbox{C/meter}, and H_x(0.8,t) = 140\pi e^{-0.15 t}\cos(0.8 \pi) = 140e^{-0.15t}\pi \cos\mathopen{}\left(\pi \cdot 0.8\right)\quad {}^\circ\hbox{C/meter}. The practical interpretation of these partial derivatives is the rate of change in temperature at x=0.2 and x=0.8 as we increase the distance from the end x=0. Notice that e^{-0.15 t} is positive for all t. Given the formula for H(x,t), we see that the closer the position to the center of the rod, the hotter the temperature. The partial derivative H_x(0.2,t) has a positive sign because, at x=0.2 as we increase x, we get closer to the center of the rod, which is hottest. The partial derivative H_x(0.8,t) has a negative sign because, at x=0.8, as we increase x, we get further away from the center of the rod which is hottest.
(b) To calculate H_t(x,t), we hold x constant and differentiate with respect to t: \frac{\partial H}{\partial t}=\frac{\partial}{\partial t}(140e^{-0.15t}\sin\mathopen{}\left(\pi x\right)) = -21e^{-0.15t}\sin\mathopen{}\left(\pi x\right)\quad {}^\circ\hbox{C/second}. For all t, and for 0\lt x\lt 1 (that is, for all t and all x inside the rod), the partial derivative H_t(x,t) is negative. In terms of heat, H_t(x,t) represents the rate at which the temperature of the rod is changing as time passes at position x and time t. Thus, the temperature inside the rod is always decreasing.
